Living Well / Practical guide

Turn scattered notes into one useful next step

Practical guide · 4 min read · Published October 10, 2026

On this page
  1. What you will make
  2. Choose a small enough pile
  3. Use three headings before adding a tool
  4. Give AI a bounded job, when useful
  5. Put the result where you will actually use it
  6. Finish with an action, not another round of organizing
  7. A small template to use
  8. One question to take with you
  9. Sources and context

By Nolan Kido · About this writing

A useful note is not the one that captures everything. It is the one that lets you recognize what matters next, without turning every thought into an obligation.

Technology for real life · Worked guide

What you will make

One short working note and one deliberate next action.

Start with: A short set of your own non-sensitive notes, with an untouched copy.

Simplest route: Use three headings in a paper or digital note. AI grouping is optional.

Finish when: You can name one next action and trace it back to the original note without inventing a deadline.

No generative AI required. Worked examples illustrate the method; they are not reports of personal tests.

Save the blank worksheet (.txt)

Choose a small enough pile

Begin with one set of low-stakes notes: a few ideas from a project, errands you have been carrying in your head, or things you meant to ask. Do not start by importing your entire inbox or years of journals. The intended result is a short working note, not a complete personal operating system.

Keep the original before changing it. A copy gives you something to check when a summary sounds plausible but misses a detail. Leave private correspondence, passwords, sensitive records, and other people's information out of an optional AI request.

Use three headings before adding a tool

On paper or in a note you already know how to open, write Next action, Keep for reference, and Question to resolve. Move each item only when its meaning is clear. You can leave something unclassified or decide it no longer deserves attention.

Fictional example: a note says, "Ask Lee whether the book swap is still happening. Bring a small box if it is. Save the article about repairing things. Maybe write about the pleasure of keeping an old object. Organize every folder someday." None of these details describes a real event or person in Nolan's life.

An adequate result is: Next action: ask whether the book swap is happening. Reference: save the article link. Question: decide whether the writing idea is worth developing. The box remains conditional. Organizing every folder can be left for later rather than promoted into a new commitment.

Give AI a bounded job, when useful

For a longer non-sensitive list, an optional prompt is: Group these notes under Next action, Reference, and Question to resolve. Preserve conditions and uncertainty. Do not add deadlines, priorities, promises, or tasks that are not in the notes. Flag ambiguous items instead of deciding what I meant.

The example above is an editorial illustration, not an executed model response. A prompt expresses what you are requesting; it does not certify the result. Compare each proposed action with the original and remove invented urgency. A phrase such as "maybe" must not disappear merely because the output looks cleaner.

Put the result where you will actually use it

Choose one familiar location rather than saving competing versions in a chat, a notebook, and three apps. Give the note an ordinary title you would search for later. When a real date is confirmed, enter it in the calendar or reminder system you already trust and check that it was saved correctly.

A portable copy can be useful. For example, Joplin documents export options including HTML and a re-importable JEX archive. That is an option for existing users, not a reason to move all your notes. Test an exported copy before relying on it; a format name alone does not establish that another person can use it.

Finish with an action, not another round of organizing

Close the note and ask whether you can name the next step. Then either take that step, deliberately schedule it, or decide not to pursue it. For the fictional list, another generated plan is less useful than actually asking about the event.

Review the method after a few ordinary uses. Did it reduce repeated searching or just produce longer lists? Count the effort spent preparing and checking an AI request. A paper note or a simpler digital list is a successful choice when it does the job with less work.

A small template to use

Use these headings on paper or copy them into your own note. Keep the answers with you; there is nothing to submit to this website.

Read or select the plain-text template
ORIGINAL NOTES
[Keep a copy here or record where they are.]

NEXT ACTION
[What I have actually decided to do.]

KEEP FOR REFERENCE
[The useful detail and where to find its source.]

QUESTION TO RESOLVE
[What is unknown, conditional, or still a possibility.]

LEAVE FOR LATER
[Something that does not need to become a task.]

CHECK
Did I keep every condition, uncertainty, and genuine commitment?
Can I close this note and name the next step?

Save the blank worksheet (.txt). The download is the exact blank text shown above, not your answers.

One question to take with you

Which item needs your attention, and which only needs a safe place to wait?
